subject: Split-path access architecture evaluation: VPC peering vs private endpoints vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Camila Reyes <camila@redwood.com>
To: Marta López <marta.lopez@finport.com>, Raj Patel <raj.patel@finport.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-04-20T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Split-path access architecture evaluation: VPC peering vs private endpoints vs S2S VPN

Hi Marta / Raj —

Thanks for the walkthrough earlier. Per our conversation I captured three realistic on-ramp patterns for a Redwood Private deployment and attached a one-page summary (redwood_split_path_summary.pdf). High level:

- Path A: VPC peering (direct routing between customer VPC and Redwood VPC) — low latency, simple routing, but requires cross-account peering and can be limited at scale for multi-region setups.
- Path B: Private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink / provider-hosted endpoint) — strong isolation, per-service endpoints, no transitive routing; slightly higher egress overhead and endpoint management.
- Path C: Site-to-site VPN (IPSec tunnel to customer on-prem) — easiest for legacy firewalls and fixed IPs, higher latency, and less bandwidth predictability.

Questions for you so we can recommend a primary and fallback path:
1) Do you need cross-VPC routing between FinPort data plane and other internal services, or will access be strictly from your app gateway to the Redwood inference endpoints?
2) Expected sustained throughput (RPS / Mbps) for model inference traffic and burst characteristics?
3) Compliance requirements: is use of managed endpoints (PrivateLink) preferred for egress minimization, or is customer-managed network peering required by your security team?

Action: if you can confirm answers to 1-3, we’ll produce a recommendation with a migration checklist and an estimated cost/latency delta for each path. I also sketched a candidate split-path design (see finport_infra_diagram_v1.png) where we use PrivateLink for control-plane and low-latency peering for high-throughput dataplane — this hybrid option can give the best of both worlds in many cases.

Thanks,
Camila
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Split-path access architecture evaluation: VPC peering vs private endpoints vs S2S VPN

Camila — thanks for the clear summary and the visuals, very helpful. Quick answers below.

1) Routing: we only need app-gateway -> Redwood inference endpoints; we do not plan to route other FinPort VPCs through Redwood. No transitive routing required.
2) Throughput: baseline 75 RPS with median response sizes that translate to ~20 Mbps sustained, with occasional spikes up to 300 RPS for short periods (less than 10 minutes).
3) Compliance: Security team prefers "no public egress" and wants strong isolation. Managed endpoints (PrivateLink) are looked upon favorably because they reduce exposed IPs and allow tighter controls.

We’re leaning toward PrivateLink but concerned about the per-endpoint cost and limits; curious whether a mixed approach (PrivateLink for control plane + peering for dataplane) makes sense for our traffic profile. Also tagging Ben and Lauren for any cost/ops concerns.

Regards,
Marta López
Head of Cloud Ops, FinPort Systems

From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Split-path access architecture evaluation: VPC peering vs private endpoints vs S2S VPN

Thanks for the details Marta — that throughput profile clarifies things. A few engineering points and an alternative we should call out:

- PrivateLink (per-service ENI/endpoint) is excellent for isolation and meets the "no public egress" ask. For the traffic numbers you quoted, a single NLB + PrivateLink endpoint should be fine for baseline, but you need to plan for concurrency limits and endpoint bandwidth. There are per-AZ ENI limits that can surface in large-scale spikes.

- VPC Peering would give lower steady-state latency (no extra NLB hop) and is simpler for steady 1:1 VPCs, but since FinPort doesn't need transitive routing and prefers isolation, peering is less attractive operationally. Also peering requires routing table management and cross-account acceptance steps.

- S2S VPN is a fallback option for on-prem legacy or when customers cannot accept provider-managed endpoints. Latency and throughput are the tradeoffs; good for bursty, low-throughput use but not great for sustained high QPS.

- Hybrid proposal (what Camila suggested): use PrivateLink for control-plane requests (auth, metadata, admin calls) and use a dedicated peered VPC for bulk inference data-plane if the customer is willing to accept peering for strictly inference traffic. That reduces per-endpoint costs and keeps control calls isolated.

Operational checklist items:
1) If PrivateLink primary: confirm endpoint quotas per account and request increases proactively.
2) If peering fallback: exchange account IDs and CIDR ranges, confirm non-overlapping subnets, and prepare route table & security group templates.
3) Monitoring: add per-path latency SLOs and automatic failover to VPN if we detect endpoint congestion or AZ-level issues.

I’ll draft a short recommendation doc that quantifies expected latency delta and rough monthly cost for the hybrid and PrivateLink-only options. Camila — want me to include a failure-mode runbook?

—Ben
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Agree with Ben. A couple of practical notes from the onboarding side:
- Provisioning time: PrivateLink onboarding (including NLB configuration) is typically 2-3 business days plus any quota increases; peering usually takes <1 day once both teams accept.
- Docs/workflows: I'll attach a checklist template (I used this previously) under the drive link so FinPort can walk security and networking teams through required approvals.

Next steps for us / FinPort:
- Marta / Raj: confirm whether FinPort security wants endpoint isolation only or both isolation + lowest latency for inference.
- If endpoint-first: provide the AWS account numbers, desired endpoint scope (one per region), and any egress rules.
- Camila / Ben: I’ll pull together the cost estimate (monthly) for PrivateLink-only vs hybrid peering + endpoint.

Thanks — happy to set a 30-min technical runbook call after we get the account numbers.

Lauren Bishop
Head of Solutions Onboarding, Redwood Inference
